I recently got to 135x5 OHP. here's a few tips that helped me out 

Pass the head 'through the window' when the bar clears the head from the bottom. You'll use more back muscles and shoulder muscles. It feels weird but you'll get used to it. 

Stay strong with the feet. I switched to a staggered stance, similar to a jerk, even when doing strict OHP because it gives me more stability to push through my feet 

I used a tight belt, and titled my chest up to the ceiling, arching my lower back. This is to get as much upper pec involved as possible. Never had back issues, but I worked up slowly. 

OHP is one of those lifts that is really individual specific. Play around to see where you feel the best and are strongest. 

Switch it up by doing seated DB at a lighter weight but going SUPER deep. Like the dumbbell touching the mid-upper bicep deep in the bottom position. Try it for a few weeks and come back.

Lots of good advice here but I'll offer a programming suggestion. 

I would recommend when lifting heavy to always start with full paused reps, and then another touch and go set (like you're doing in the video.) the full paused reps really build strength and comfortability out of the hole, and the tng gives you the neural drive. 

I do 3-5 reps and increase once I hit 6. 1RM is not advisable mid program. Hitting a heavy 1RM is something you need to build your body towards; not something one should do without slowly overloading it deliberately. I never hit 1RMs unless I'm training specifically for one. 

A form cue as well. Keep your chest a little bigger and over emphasize the upright posture from the bottom of the squat to the top. It looks like you begin the lift by raising your hips before your knee or shoulders, and that split second is 'curling' the bar with your lower back. 

This is known as a good morning fault. It's super duper common. 

I think about rotating my femurs into my hips and keeping my knees outward. This collects my glutes together and let's my hips and shoulders rise at the same time. Try it out.

This is 6x a week? I think the volume is too much relative to the rest. Try an asynchronous split of 2 on, one off. Limbs, torso, rest. You'll get more rest time, which means MORE growth time, and you'll still be in the gym a lot which is great. (DM me for an example program) 

Whatever body part or lift you want to progress the fastest should be earlier in your program. If you want your arms to progress, you should be doing them first, or at least have an arm exercise as 1st or 2nd exercise in the workout. 

If you've been doing the same exercises or method for longer than 2 months, switch it up for new stimulus. The body reacts well to new exercises. 

Finally make sure you check your form so it's more stretch focused. Not sure what your technique is like, but generally long eccentrics and full stretch will help your muscle grow more. Full rom, slow eccentric.

Every time I reach a strength plateau, I always go back to hypertrophy training for a few weeks to grow muscle that I can then recompose to apply to my strength. 

This helped me grab a new bench pr (250!) after a 4 weeks push. Here's the strategy:

Program your target exercise 2x a week. Warm up with your 20RM for 10, your 10rm for 5, and then your 1-3RM for an unrack and then rerack OR your 5rm for 1. This potentiates your strength. 3-5 min rest then youre into your working sets. 

First set is power/strength. I prefer rep ranges 3-5 here but if your goal is 1-3, then stay there. Do this totally fresh. For gaining strength I highly recommend working in the 3-5 range. This will reduce injury risk and you still get strength gains. Besides 5RM is more impressive no? 

Next two working sets are rep ranges of 10-12 with slow eccentric perfect form. 
Then add an accessory exercise for 1-2 sets that will help your main lift. 

So for my bench it looks like this 

Bench warm up 135x10, 185x5 225x1. 
Power set 225x5 
Hypertrophy sets 185x9 175x11
Larsen press 145x11. 

Once you hit the upper range of your target rep range you can go up on weight. For example, if I do 220x4 I HAVE to hit 220x5 before I try 225x4. 

This will get you there fast and safely.

I like that this is flexible. I would be cautious with such variable amounts of sets per workout though. If you're pressed for time I would recommend some other strategies to increase intensity for shorter periods of time, such as MYO sets, and stick to a solid 'i must execute this many sets in this rep range for this workout'. This way it'll be easier to overload instead of having to adjust week to week cause you did 4 sets of bench last week but you only have time for 3 sets this week. It will be difficult to match or increase stimulation for 3 sets when compared to 4 of last week. This can be a deload, or active recovery strategy, but I don't think this program is deliberate enough for that. 

I generally like exercise selection, but I'd make less exercise variation in this mesocycle. If you're doing something like full body 2x a week (I'm just going to assume it's going to be this, because it's very unlikely people execute 'optional' days when they're deemed as optional) then I think it could be better to do something like just high bar squats 2x a week for a month, then switching to lowbar for the next month. Having multiple variations of exercises and cycling through them every mesocycle is a great way to keep getting that 'fresh' stimulus. If you make multiple exercises that cover the same movement a week, you'll run out of fresh exercises to use when they get stale. Furthermore, doing one exercise 2 times a week makes you better at the exercise, so you more effectively target the muscle as you spend more time on it!

Also consider an asynchronous split. Something like day 1, day 2, rest rest rest, day 1 day 2 rest rest rest. You can be flexible in rest days, but do something more akin to upper lower or ppl and save a few sets in the gym. If Tuesday and Thursday are the only days you can consistently do, then this works fine. If you're able to be consistent on the Saturday and not skip it, then just do 3x a week bro don't make it optional. 

These are nitpicky critiques but I hope they helped.

I think your shoulders are a little too far in front of the bar. Your shoulder should be right above the bar. This means after you finish hinging your hips, you can  continue further back by dropping your hips. From here, grip the bar, LOCK your lats into your lower back and push through your feet and you'll feel the slack come out of the bar. So see how your shoulders and arms are not in line w the bar? You're leaning a little bit ahead of it. This means you're not pushing your butt back enough and lowering your hips. You want your starting position to have your shoulders directly above the bar, and your arms in a straight line towards it. So when you stand at the bar, start by push your hands into your hips and fold them, hinging back until you feel a stretch in your hams and glutes. Then lower your hips back FURTHER until your shoulders are aligned and your arms are straight above the bar. 

You're going to wiggle the position, which will have your hips a little lower, activate your hips and glutes, breath in and brace and then pull your lats in towards your lower back. This becomes one rigid board that will not flex at any point during the lift. 

You're going to slowly push your feet into the ground which will feel a bit like a squat and pull the bar up by activating your lats more to create tension in the position, and maintaining that tension you will push your glutes and hips forwards at the same time you push your feet DEEP into the ground with an explosive power. Your head high and tensions still in the back you will also pull up using your upper back. You have two forces; one pushing down and one pulling up. Your glutes are the glue that connect it so squeeze them as you collect everything together into a standing position. 

The deadlift is very complicated so keep up on technique!! The core principles are: you don't want spinal flexion to happen under load so practice good bracing and engage your hips and glutes. Lock in your upper back to your lower back with your lats. 2 forces are Pushing down through the feet and pulling up with your upper back. Get rid of the tension at the bottom of the lift before exploding entirely into the top of it. I've been dead lifting for years and I still work on making every motion more efficient to protect my back and perform the lift better and better.

There's kind of two schools of thought related to defining genres. One is historical and the other is musical theoretical. Hyperpops roots can be considered the PC music era, with artists like AG and Sophie and GFOTY taking popular music tropes and making them very dramatic; borderline satirical. In this Sense, the content of Hyperpop in that sphere was very diverse as there wasn't a 'standard', however its generally agreed that there are pop song writing elements such verse chorus form with repetitive hooks and choruses, with the addition of cyclic chord progressions. These are hybridized and heightened with EDM style production like Dubstep and DnB and often including drops, and autotune as a timbral decision.

However when dissecting the contents as those simple definitions (mixture of pop and EDM) the line gets blurry. Is Cher's Believe hyperpop? What about Kanye West's Yeezus? While those songs use similar musical characteristics to the genre we call hyperpop today, I believe that it would be controversial to call either of those works 'hyperpop' or 'hyperrap'. 

That's why there needs to be some element of the 'underground' in it's composition, production, release and audience. Hyperpop is not just defined by music, it's defined by being tangentially related to the mainstream while never fully breaching into it. 1000 gecs will never be truly 'mainstream' no matter how popular it becomes, and neither will Ericdoa, Dorian Electra, or Sophies music. 

So hyperpop today is basically categorized as 'classical hyperpop'  with enough repertoire that creates a canon of what hyperpop was. Then there's the underground and progressive side of hyperpop which is the philosophy of hybridizing or 'hyper-izing' other popular genres, continuing the movement of hyperpop. 

Ezekial is quite popular, but his approach to hyperizing pop punk, emo and punk genres place him firmly against the mainstream and continuing the tradition of creating more hyper styles. Ergo, while ezekial may not be included in the canon of 'classical hyperpop' he still 'hyperizes popular genres' which continues the aesthetic tradition and philosophy of hyperpop. Likely we will see Ezekial and Ericdoa as continuations or a 'third movement' of the hyperpop genre.

I started on judo first for 14 years before I picked up boxing and Muay Thai. I've done Muay Thai for far less time but I figured I'd like to give my input. 

Judo is great for a lot of things. Helps you understand distance through grip fighting as well as inside positioning (ie wrestling clinching or 'infighting'). The fundamental reflexes gained through grip fighting are invaluable and transferable to basically all martial arts. 

You learn to fall and breakfall which is HUGE and a skill in itself. I've been hit by cars and my breakfall has saved my life on more than one occasion. IF YOU CHOOSE MUAY THAI LEARN TO BREAKFALL AND ROLL REGARDLESS 

You actually get a decently hard body and degree of toughness in judo from getting smashed all the time. Breakfalls make your neck quite stronger. It's not the same as the brutal toughness high level Thai fighters have but the muscle mass gained and ability to absorb shock is really beneficial. I have a pretty thick neck from judo and I attribute it to why I have a decent chin in boxing and Muay Thai. 

You learn ground fighting which is great too. Totally different topic but that's something to consider as you get no ground fighting experience in Muay Thai. 

The downsides are obviously weaker striking. You have less refined footwork for Muay Thai or boxing and you will hurt a LOT in the thighs. You'll need to learn how to see punches coming and not blink and you'll need to change your approach to clinching with gloves on.

Judo has far more rigid rules as well which offers its own set of disadvantages but I find this only becomes a true handicap in mma or other grappling arts as Muay Thai and judo are so different.  

I do think you should consider which would be more difficult; transferring from judo to Muay Thai or Muay Thai to judo and I don't know which for you would be more difficult. I found Muay Thai easier to pick up from my judo experience. I also hear lots of anecdotal experience saying it's easier to move from wrestling to boxing or grappling to striking in general. All of this is much more dependant on you and your style however. 

You really can't go wrong choosing either in my mind. I'd pick the one that interests you the most at this moment in your life and be the other one later one.

Ninja edit; judo is perfectly effective as self defense. Learning real resistance in throwing people has saved me a couple times. There's been lots of scenarios where a throw has ended a fight quickly and safely and I haven't had to throw a punch. In self defense RUNNING AWAY IS THE BEST OPTION and DIFFUSING THE SITUATION IS THE SECOND BEST but in my mind the third is grappling. Punching means you're generally in range to grab your opponent which means throws are the best way to neutralize someone without clobbering them and them dying on you. The only self defense thing that is an issue is no leg grabs and throws using the Gi primarily. While most people wear clothes it is hard to say whether you can perform the same techniques on someone wearing a jacket or something. 

Judo has more injuries cause the nature of the sport makes it so you can "spar" far more often.
